subject: Critical Thinking
title: The Framing Effect: Same Facts, Different Decisions
description: A quick win: understand The Framing Effect: Same Facts, Different Decisions.

hook.text: 'This yogurt is 90% fat-free' or 'This yogurt contains 10% fat.' Same yogurt. Completely different sales.

buildup.text: The framing effect: how information is presented changes decisions — even when the underlying facts are identical.

discovery.text: Tversky & Kahneman: '200 of 600 people saved' vs.

twist.text: Gain frames make people conservative. Loss frames make people reckless. Marketers and politicians know this.

climax.text: The antidote: reframe every major decision both ways. If your choice changes, the framing was doing the thinking.

punchline.text: The frame isn't the picture. Don't let it choose for you.

quiz.question: What does the framing effect demonstrate?
options: How information is presented changes decisions even with identical facts

details.summary: The framing effect shows that identical information presented differently leads to different decisions. A treatment with a 90% survival rate sounds appealing; a 10% mortality rate sounds risky. Same fact, opposite feelings.
details.whyItMatters: Framing is used in politics, medicine, and marketing to guide your choices. Recognizing frames lets you strip away the spin and evaluate the actual information.
takeaways: Presenting gains versus losses changes decisions dramatically
Framing exploits loss aversion and emotional processing
Translating claims into both positive and negative frames reveals bias

faq.question: How does the framing effect influence medical decisions?
faq.answer: Patients told a surgery has a 90% survival rate are more likely to choose it than when told it has a 10% mortality rate. Doctors who understand framing present both versions to help patients decide rationally.

faq.question: What is the simplest technique to counteract the framing effect?
faq.answer: Restate the information in the opposite frame. If you hear '95% fat-free,' reframe it as '5% fat.' If both versions lead to the same judgment, your decision is frame-independent and more rational.
